title: Glee Star Kevin McHale Blasts Fans Calling Show Cursed: ‘Get F--ked’
excerpt: The actor condemned those who reduce the deaths of three cast members to a TV show curse, calling the rhetoric 'diabolical and untethered from humanity.'
body:
• Kevin McHale, who played Artie Abrams on Glee, posted an angry rebuke on X against fans who call the show cursed
  • Three main cast members — Cory Monteith, Mark Salling, and Naya Rivera — died between 2013 and 2020
  • McHale called the rhetoric around their deaths as "sacrifices" or "curses" diabolical and untethered from reality
  • The post follows years of social media conspiracy theories treating real tragedies as entertainment mythology

Glee star Kevin McHale erupted at fans on Wednesday, condemning those who continue to call the hit Fox show cursed following the deaths of three of its main cast members.

The 38-year-old actor, who played wheelchair-using singer Artie Abrams across all six seasons of the musical comedy-drama, posted a blunt message on X that left little room for interpretation.

"The way too many of you talk about real people who have passed as a 'sacrifice' or a 'curse' in regards to a tv show is f--king diabolical and untethered from any sort of humanity or reality. Get f--ked."

— Kevin McHale, via X

Three Deaths, Years of Conspiracies

The "Glee curse" narrative has persisted on social media for years, treating the deaths of Cory Monteith, Mark Salling, and Naya Rivera as interconnected elements of a supernatural pattern rather than individual tragedies.

Monteith, who played quarterback Finn Hudson, died of a heroin overdose in a Vancouver hotel room on July 13, 2013. He was 31.

Salling, who played jock Noah "Puck" Puckerman, died by suicide in January 2018 at age 35, a month after pleading guilty to possession of child pornography.

Rivera, who portrayed cheerleader Santana Lopez, drowned on July 13, 2020, at age 33, after using all her strength to push her then-4-year-old son Josey back onto a rented pontoon boat on Lake Piru in Ventura County, California. Though she saved her son's life, she did not survive.

Fans Rally Behind McHale

The response to McHale's post was largely supportive. "It's a reminder that real tragedies aren't plot devices," one user wrote. "Turning someone's death into 'proof' of a curse or a TV show's mythology can erase the fact that they were actual people with families, friends, and lives beyond the entertainment people consumed."

Others expressed surprise that the curse narrative persists. "People are still going on about the whole 'curse' thing?" one user wrote.

McHale has addressed the topic before, though less forcefully. In a 2024 podcast appearance, he said he did not believe in curses but acknowledged the weight of the losses: "If we don't laugh about this, we will all just be sad because it's insane."

The outburst underscores a growing tension between social media's appetite for true-crime and conspiracy content and the real people left to grieve. For a show that at its peak attracted more than 10 million viewers and became a cultural touchstone for a generation, the legacy has been increasingly shadowed by tragedy and its online commodification.
nri_angle: The story highlights broader tensions between social media conspiracy culture and real grief that resonate across global fandoms.
author: Diaspora Desk
